lead: Boundary scan puts a small test cell at every digital signal pin of a chip and a serial controller inside it, so a whole board of chips can be tested through four wires: TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO. The standard is IEEE 1149.1, usually called JTAG. It checks the wiring between chips after soldering, not the logic inside them, and the same port is used to program flash and FPGAs on the board and to reach a chip's internal test hardware.
prereq: You need: shift registers and scan cells from 6.4, and the board-test step from 6.1.

sections.h3: The test access port and the boundary cells

blocks.text: JTAG adds a test access port (TAP) to the chip. Four pins are required: TCK, the test clock; TMS, test mode select, which steers the TAP controller; TDI, serial test data in; and TDO, serial test data out. TMS and TDI are sampled on the rising edge of TCK, and TDO changes on the falling edge, so the next device in a chain samples a steady bit. A fifth pin, TRST, an asynchronous reset, is optional.

A boundary-scan cell sits between the core logic and each digital signal pad (power, ground and analog pins have none). In normal mode the cell is transparent. In test mode an output cell can drive its pad from a stored bit, and an input cell can capture the value arriving at its pad. All the cells join into one shift register, the boundary-scan register (BSR).

Why at the pin? Inside the chip, scan and BIST do the testing. The copper trace between two chips on a board has no access point once fine-pitch and ball-grid-array parts are soldered, and a bed-of-nails fixture cannot reach it. Boundary scan moves the probe to the pin: the tester shifts a pattern into the output cells, the chips drive the traces, and the input cells capture what arrives. A wrong bit shows an open trace, a short to a neighbour or a missing part.

The TAP controller is a 16-state machine that moves on each rising edge of TCK according to TMS. Besides Test-Logic-Reset and Run-Test/Idle it has two matching columns of seven states, one for a data register (DR) and one for the instruction register (IR): Select, Capture, Shift, Exit1, Pause, Exit2 and Update. Capture loads the register in parallel, Shift moves it one bit per TCK from TDI to TDO, and Update copies the shifted bits to the outputs. Holding TMS = 1 for five TCK edges reaches Test-Logic-Reset from any state.

Every compliant chip has the instruction register (IR, at least 2 bits), the 1-bit bypass register and the BSR; most also have a 32-bit IDCODE register that returns the maker and part number. The instruction in the IR decides which data register sits between TDI and TDO.

head: Instruction
Register between TDI and TDO
What it does
rows: Passes data through a chip that is not being tested
Captures pin values without disturbing normal operation; loads a safe pattern before EXTEST
Output cells drive the pins and input cells capture them: the board-wiring test
Shifts out the identity of the chip
Applies values to the core logic through the boundary cells

blocks.text: On a board the chips form a daisy chain: the board's TDI goes to the first chip's TDI, each TDO feeds the next TDI, and the last TDO is the board's TDO. TCK and TMS go to every chip in parallel, so all TAP controllers step through the same states together and the board behaves as one long shift register.

blocks.where: where L is the number of bits shifted in one pass of Shift-IR or Shift-DR and Lᵢ is the length of the register selected in chip i. The bits for the chip nearest TDO are shifted in first.

blocks.text: In an interconnect test the tester loads EXTEST into every chip, preloads drive values, then for each pattern captures the received bits and shifts them out while the next pattern shifts in. A short changes the captured bit of both nets; an open leaves the receiving pin floating, so its bit is unreliable. In-system programming uses the same port: the FPGA or flash is put in programming mode and its configuration is shifted through TDI and TDO.

spec.aria: State diagram of the JTAG TAP controller with Test-Logic-Reset, Run-Test/Idle, and the seven DR and seven IR states, with TMS values on each arrow and the worked-example path highlighted.

examples.question: A board carries three JTAG chips in a daisy chain. Their instruction registers are 4, 4 and 5 bits; their boundary-scan registers are 20, 20 and 30 cells. Starting in Test-Logic-Reset, the tester loads EXTEST into all three chips and then shifts one complete boundary-scan pattern. (a) How many bits pass in Shift-IR and in Shift-DR? (b) Write the TMS sequence. (c) How many TCK cycles does the whole job take?
steps: (a) Shift-IR: 4 + 4 + 5 = 13 bits. Shift-DR with EXTEST selects the BSRs: 20 + 20 + 30 = 70 bits. (With BYPASS in all three it would be 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 bits.)
Shift 13 instruction bits: TMS = 0 for 12 edges and 1 on the 13th, which shifts the last bit and moves to Exit1-IR. Then TMS = 1 (Update-IR): EXTEST becomes active.
From Update-IR: TMS = 1 (Select-DR), 0 (Capture-DR, the input cells capture the pins), 0 (Shift-DR): 3 edges.
Shift 70 data bits: TMS = 0 for 69 edges and 1 on the 70th (to Exit1-DR). Then TMS = 1 (Update-DR, the output cells drive the new pattern) and 0 (Run-Test/Idle).
examples.answer: 13 instruction bits and 70 data bits; TMS = 0 1 1 0 0, then twelve 0s and a 1, then 1 1 0 0, then sixty-nine 0s and a 1, then 1 0; 94 TCK cycles in all, or 9.4 µs at a 10 MHz TCK.

traps: Thinking boundary scan tests the logic inside the chip. It tests pins and board wiring; the core needs scan or BIST.
Using one chip's IR length for the board. In a daisy chain the instruction lengths add, and so do the selected data-register lengths.
Forgetting that the last shift happens on the edge that leaves Shift-DR: n bits need n edges in the Shift state, the last with TMS = 1.
Saying SAMPLE/PRELOAD drives the board. It only captures pin values and preloads the cells; EXTEST drives.
Treating TMS as a data pin. TDI and TDO carry data, TMS steers the state machine, TCK clocks both.

quiz.q: Name the four required JTAG pins and the optional fifth one.
quiz.a: TCK test clock, TMS test mode select, TDI test data in, TDO test data out; TRST, the asynchronous test reset, is optional.

quiz.q: Which three instructions must every IEEE 1149.1 chip have?
quiz.a: BYPASS, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST. IDCODE and INTEST are optional.

quiz.q: What does the bypass register do, and why is it only one bit?
quiz.a: It puts a single flip-flop between TDI and TDO for a chip that is not being tested, so data crosses that chip in one TCK instead of its whole BSR.

quiz.q: Why are TMS and TDI sampled on the rising edge of TCK while TDO changes on the falling edge?
quiz.a: The half period between the falling edge, where a chip's TDO changes, and the next rising edge, where the next chip samples it as TDI, gives the bit time to settle, so a daisy chain works without hold-time races.

quiz.q: Three chips have IR lengths 3, 5 and 4 bits and are all given BYPASS. How many TCK edges in Shift-IR and how many in Shift-DR are needed to pass one bit through?
quiz.a: Shift-IR: 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 edges. Shift-DR through three bypass registers: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 edges.

quiz.q: From any unknown state, how does the tester reach Run-Test/Idle?
quiz.a: Hold TMS = 1 for five TCK edges to reach Test-Logic-Reset, then give one edge with TMS = 0. Six edges in all.

quiz.q: In an EXTEST run, a trace between two chips captures 0 where 1 is expected. Give two physical causes and say which gives a dependable 0.
quiz.a: A short to ground, or a short to a neighbouring net that is driving 0 (a wired-AND short), gives a dependable 0. An open trace leaves the receiving pin floating, so it may read 0, 1 or its last value; that is why interconnect codes avoid relying on a single bit.

beyond: Not for the exam. JTAG is also the debug port of most processors, giving run control and memory access, which is why shipped products often lock it. IEEE 1149.7 cuts the port to two wires, and IEEE 1687 (IJTAG) gives access to embedded instruments behind the TAP. Search 'TAP state diagram', 'IJTAG' and 'JTAG security'.
